m4-t1.introduction: Understand paid media as an amplifier, not a repair service. Read the auction conceptually and run the campaign arithmetic before spending.

sections.title: Paid traffic multiplies what is already there
sections.explanation: Ads can bring attention quickly. They also expose a weak offer, irrelevant page or broken tracking more quickly.

items.label: Offer
items.detail: Confirm the customer need and a credible promise.

items.label: Destination
items.detail: Make the page and next action work.

items.label: Measurement
items.detail: Test the event that represents business value.

items.label: Amplify
items.detail: Buy appropriate distribution with a controlled plan.

sections.takeaway: A budget cannot make an unwanted or confusing offer automatically useful.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.

sections.title: Relevance can beat a larger bid
sections.explanation: Use this comparison to understand the direction of the trade-off, not to calculate a real auction result.

items.label: Larger bid, weaker fit
items.detail: A generic ad points to a home page that does not answer the query.

items.label: Smaller bid, stronger fit
items.detail: The ad and landing page answer the same specific need.

items.label: Real auction context
items.detail: Platforms also consider thresholds, context, expected impact and other signals.

sections.takeaway: Bid × quality is a teaching simplification. Google Quality Score is diagnostic; it is not a literal input you can multiply to reproduce Ad Rank.
sections.caption: Conceptual auction comparison. This is not a pricing formula, platform simulator or promise of cheaper clicks.

sections.title: Billing and optimisation are not the same thing
sections.explanation: Know both what is billed and what the bidding system is trying to achieve.

items.label: CPC
items.detail: Spend is expressed per click; useful for traffic cost reasoning.

items.label: CPM
items.detail: Spend is expressed per thousand impressions; useful for exposure cost reasoning.

items.label: Target CPA / value
items.detail: The system optimises toward actions or value; actual billing and eligibility depend on the platform.

sections.takeaway: Selecting a target CPA does not generally mean you only pay when someone converts. Check the actual billing terms.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.
sections.section: 3. Formats and buying models — the vocabulary

sections.title: The paid pre-flight chain
sections.explanation: This synthetic example follows the reading: ₹6,000 ÷ ₹12 CPC = 500 clicks; at 4%, that is 20 expected orders and ₹300 media CPA.

items.label: Clicks
items.detail: ₹6,000 budget divided by ₹12 assumed CPC.

items.label: Expected orders
items.detail: 4% of 500 clicks.

sections.takeaway: A ₹300 CPA is not automatically profitable. Include contribution margin, refunds, fulfilment and other acquisition costs in the verdict.
sections.caption: Synthetic worked example, not live campaign data or an industry benchmark.

checkpoint.question: Does choosing target CPA guarantee paying only for conversions?
checkpoint.answer: No. Target CPA is usually an optimisation goal, not a universal billing rule. Confirm how the selected platform charges and verify conversion tracking first.

m4-t2.introduction: Keep the search query, ad group, message and landing page aligned. Protect the budget with exclusions and diagnose outcomes after the click.

sections.title: Organise around a coherent intent
sections.explanation: A campaign groups the budget and objective. Ad groups keep related queries and messages close together.

items.label: Campaign
items.detail: One business objective, geography and budget logic.

items.label: Ad group
items.detail: A tightly related theme such as weekend coaching.

items.label: Keywords / ads
items.detail: Use query-relevant language and useful variants.

items.label: Landing page
items.detail: Answer that same promise with a clear action.

sections.takeaway: A tidy account structure makes performance easier to interpret; structure alone does not create demand.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.

sections.title: Match types open the door; negatives guard it
sections.explanation: Broadness is a reach choice. Negative keywords help filter irrelevant demand, but exclusions need review too.

items.label: Broader reach
items.detail: More possible queries; potentially more discovery and waste.

items.label: Tighter intent
items.detail: More focused query matching; still inspect actual search terms.

items.label: Negative shield
items.detail: Exclude irrelevant needs such as jobs when selling a course.

sections.takeaway: Match behaviour evolves. Review current platform documentation and actual queries rather than relying on punctuation alone.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.
sections.section: 2. Match types and the negative shield

sections.title: The ad should answer the query
sections.explanation: Use the limited space to show relevance, a supported reason to choose you and a clear destination.

items.label: Query
items.detail: “Weekend CA Foundation classes Mysuru”.

items.label: Message
items.detail: Name the course, weekend timing and location honestly.

items.label: Proof / detail
items.detail: Use real fees, support or batch information where appropriate.

items.label: Destination
items.detail: Open the weekend-batch page, not a generic welcome page.

sections.takeaway: Do not create an attractive ad promise the landing page cannot fulfil.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.
sections.section: 3. Writing the ad: answer the query

sections.title: Read the chain, not one isolated metric
sections.explanation: A click-through improvement can still produce worse business results if the traffic is less relevant.

items.label: Search terms
items.detail: Are the queries actually relevant?

items.label: Ad response
items.detail: Do impressions become useful clicks?

items.label: Page response
items.detail: Do clicks become qualified enquiries?

items.label: Cost outcome
items.detail: Does the media CPA fit the agreed guardrail?

sections.takeaway: Check tracking, definitions and sample size before declaring a winner.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.

checkpoint.question: An ad gets many clicks but almost no qualified enquiries. What do you inspect?
checkpoint.answer: Check actual search terms, the promise-to-page match, form usability, qualification criteria and event tracking. Do not assume increasing the bid solves the problem.

m4-t3.introduction: Interruption media must earn attention before it can ask for action. Connect audience warmth, creative and exposure frequency to the campaign’s role.

sections.title: Intent capture and interruption do different jobs
sections.explanation: Someone searching for a cake is in a different moment from someone scrolling past a cake video.

items.label: Search moment
items.detail: The person is already expressing a need.

items.label: Feed / video moment
items.detail: The creative must earn attention and establish relevance.

items.label: Appropriate next step
items.detail: Match the ask to readiness rather than demanding a purchase immediately.

sections.takeaway: Judge a discovery ad on its agreed role without pretending awareness alone proves sales impact.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.
sections.section: 1. Interruption media: the job and the price

sections.title: Build an audience ladder
sections.explanation: As familiarity changes, the appropriate message changes. Respect consent and platform restrictions on audience use.

items.label: Cold audience
items.detail: Introduce a relevant problem and a credible promise.

items.label: Engaged audience
items.detail: Offer more explanation, demonstrations and proof.

items.label: High-intent audience
items.detail: Answer remaining objections and make action easier.

items.label: Existing customers
items.detail: Use helpful lifecycle communication where permitted.

sections.takeaway: Retargeting is not permission to use sensitive data or ignore opt-outs.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.
sections.section: 2. Audiences: the real levers of social

sections.title: Creative has a small sequence of jobs
sections.explanation: Good feed creative makes its meaning visible quickly, even without sound.

items.label: Hook
items.detail: Show the customer’s relevant situation.

items.label: Demonstrate
items.detail: Use visual proof or one clear explanation.

items.label: Clarify
items.detail: Make the offer and important conditions readable.

items.label: Invite
items.detail: Name a next step that matches the stage.

sections.takeaway: Test a meaningful creative hypothesis, not just a different background colour.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.

sections.title: Frequency is exposure, not a count of people
sections.explanation: If 10,000 reached people receive 40,000 impressions, average frequency is 4. It does not mean everyone saw the ad exactly four times.

items.label: Days 1–3: introduction
items.detail: First part of a synthetic sequence.

items.label: Days 4–7: demonstration
items.detail: Second part: explain value to the appropriate audience.

items.label: Days 8–10: reminder
items.detail: Third part: a useful reminder, with exclusions where appropriate.

sections.takeaway: These stages total 40,000 impressions. Monitor fatigue and useful outcomes; there is no universal ideal frequency.
sections.caption: Synthetic worked example, not live campaign data or an industry benchmark.

checkpoint.question: If average frequency is four, did every reached person see exactly four ads?
checkpoint.answer: No. It is impressions divided by reach. Exposure is distributed unevenly, so use the average with creative-fatigue signals and outcome evidence.

m4-t4.introduction: Treat the landing page, budget and tracking as one launch system. Test the measurement before the first rupee goes live.

sections.title: A landing page continues the promise
sections.explanation: Every extra distraction competes with the action the campaign was designed to support.

items.label: Recognise
items.detail: Repeat the ad’s actual offer and context.

items.label: Believe
items.detail: Show useful details and genuine proof.

items.label: Act
items.detail: Keep the form or order route simple and accessible.

items.label: Confirm
items.detail: Explain what happens next and record the intended event.

sections.takeaway: Remove friction without hiding fees, conditions or privacy information.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.
sections.section: 1. The landing page: one promise, zero friction

sections.title: Pacing is a budget control loop
sections.explanation: Compare cumulative spend with a plan. A variance is a prompt to investigate, not an automatic instruction to increase bids.

items.label: Week 1 plan
items.detail: Half of a synthetic ₹6,000 two-week budget.

items.label: Week 1 actual
items.detail: ₹1,200 above the cumulative plan.

sections.takeaway: At this point ₹1,800 remains, not ₹3,000. Check schedule, audience, CPC and results before changing the plan.
sections.caption: Synthetic worked example, not live campaign data or an industry benchmark.

sections.title: The safe launch order
sections.explanation: A conversion report is useful only after the event path is verified. Do not spend first and debug the count later.

items.label: Define
items.detail: Choose the meaningful action and event name.

items.label: Implement
items.detail: Add the event and consistent source tags.

items.label: Test
items.detail: Use a test visit and verify the event once, with expected parameters.

items.label: Launch
items.detail: Start with budget controls and a monitoring owner.

sections.takeaway: A form-button click is not the same as a successfully completed enquiry.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.
sections.section: 3. Tracking before launch — the non-negotiable order

sections.title: Check launch health before scaling
sections.explanation: Separate a technical check from a performance decision. Early weak results may also be a measurement failure.

items.label: Confirm delivery
items.detail: Check approval, targeting, dates and budget limits.

items.label: Confirm experience
items.detail: Open the ad path on a phone and complete a test action.

items.label: Confirm data
items.detail: Check source tags, event counts and duplicates.

items.label: Review rules
items.detail: Use the pre-agreed pause, revise or scale criteria.

sections.takeaway: Document the change and the reason so the first-week review has an audit trail.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.

checkpoint.question: What should happen before an ad campaign begins spending?
checkpoint.answer: Define a meaningful outcome, implement and test its tracking, check the landing path on mobile, confirm consent and budget controls, and assign a monitoring owner.
